topic: Dynamic Batch Timeouts Cripple Real-Time ML P99
postText:
Your model inference server runs at 95% GPU utilization during stress tests. Then production traffic drops at 2 AM, and your real-time latency alarms explode.

In healthcare systems where I work, diagnostic risk scoring models must return inference within 80 milliseconds. When engineers first deployed Triton Inference Server with dynamic batching, throughput looked legendary. But dynamic batching has a hidden trap: `max_queue_delay_microseconds`.

Under high load, incoming requests fill the batch buffer instantly. GPU hits full tensor parallelism. Under sparse traffic, individual urgent clinical requests sit in scheduler queues waiting for sister requests that never arrive until timeout triggers. Result: P99 latency degrades to your maximum wait ceiling.

We solved this with three architectural changes:
1. Adaptive delay backoff: Ingress rate-sensing middleware throttles queue wait times downward when request frequency falls.
2. Dual runtime scheduler: Separate fast-path single-item queues for low-latency scoring from batched batch queues for offline document parsing.
3. Early execution thresholds: Trigger tensor execution the moment minimum cost-effective tensor slice fills, ignoring static timers.

Throughput metrics lie if latency distribution ignores quiet hours.

How do you balance GPU saturation against strict SLA ceilings in your real-time inference pipelines? Do you use dynamic batching engines or isolate dedicated low-concurrency instances?
